paras: The lynching of Bob Broom was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of more than 200 men at Utica, Hinds County, Mississippi, on August 13, 1888. Broom had been jailed the night before, accused of leading a party of Black men who shot Dr. L. W. Holliday dead and wounded two other white men after a quarrel over the sidewalk. The story ran across the country, and a month later papers reported that a second accused man, Curtis Shortney, had been taken from a train and was supposed lynched.

According to Jackson dispatches, on Sunday evening, August 12, a young white man, named as Beverly Robinson or E. B. Robertson, was escorting a young lady to church when they met Broom and several Black girls on the sidewalk. The white accounts said Broom refused to give way and pushed Robertson or the lady aside, and Robertson told him he would see him again.

Late that night, while Robertson stood before a store with friends including Frank Wallace and the physician Holliday, Broom and four or five other Black men came up and opened fire, according to the white reports. Holliday was shot in the head, Armand White in the thigh and Wallace in the arm. Robertson held Broom until help came, and he was jailed while his companions fled.

The Memphis Appeal's correspondent wrote that a "legal investigation" was held at Utica the next morning; a Jackson dispatch said it "proved Broom's guilt." Between 4 and 5 o'clock that afternoon the crowd took Broom from the jail, which some dispatches called the calaboose, and hanged him at a tree near the town cemetery.

Ike Broom, described as his brother, and Sam Harris were jailed at Raymond, although the Appeal said there was no evidence against them. Raney Short and Curtis Short escaped, and a posse went after them. On September 12 a Raymond dispatch reported that Curtis Shortney, said to have been with Broom in the killing, was taken from an eastbound freight train six miles west of Utica by a party that ordered the conductor to stop. He was "supposed" lynched, but no report confirming his death was found, nor any report of an inquest or arrests.

White papers from Washington and Savannah to Sacramento and Kansas ran one of three Jackson wire versions between August 14 and 22, and the Appeal printed a longer special. Headlines presented the hanging as retribution: the Savannah Morning News wrote "Indignant Citizens Avenge the Crime Under Judge Lynch's Code," the Richmond Dispatch "A Negro Desperado Lynched," and the Maysville Evening Bulletin blamed a Negro "wanting all the sidewalk." The Appeal headlined "An Impudent and Brutal Negro" and said Utica's people were "not the sort to brook outrages of this kind without avenging them." The dispatches stressed that the white men were unarmed, though the Appeal's account said Wallace drew a pistol.

Mississippi weeklies gave the story briefly. The Okolona Chickasaw Messenger called it "another brutal killing of a white man by a negro" but said the lynching did not improve respect for law, blaming the state's "pardon shop."

The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, offered another account on September 29 under the line "The way they do it down South." It said the white man put his hands on the Black woman's shoulder to push her off the walk, and that the white men later meant to give her companion "a sound thrashing." The result, it wrote, was "a white man shot down dead in self defense, and a Negro lynched."

The white dispatches said Broom's party fired "without warning or provocation," while the Gazette described the shooting as self-defense against a planned beating. Early reports also differ on whether Holliday died instantly or was mortally wounded, and on whether the attackers numbered five or six.

bases: A crowd of more than 200 took Bob Broom from jail at Utica and hanged him (A2, A3, A17).
Broom was taken from jail by a mob of 200 or more and hanged (A2, A3), with no lawful authority, to 'avenge the diabolical outrage' of the shooting of Holliday (A3).

The Memphis Appeal special (A3), three separate Jackson wires (A1, A2, A17), the Evening Post via the Greenville Times (A18) and the Cleveland Gazette (A29) all report Broom lynched; the Gazette disputes only the provocation.
